claim: Joubert syndrome (JBTS) is a severe recessive neurodevelopmental ciliopathy which can affect several organ systems.
source: Joubert syndrome (JBTS) is a severe recessive neurodevelopmental ciliopathy which can affect several organ systems.
evidence: This is a definitional statement about JBTS that draws from established scientific knowledge about the disease.

claim: Mutations in known JBTS genes account for approximately half of the cases.
source: Mutations in known JBTS genes account for approximately half of the cases.
evidence: This statement is supported by established knowledge in the field about the genetic basis of JBTS.

claim: A novel locus, JBTS23, was identified with a homozygous splice site mutation in KIAA0586 by homozygosity mapping and whole-exome sequencing.
source: By homozygosity mapping and whole-exome sequencing, we identified a novel locus, JBTS23, with a homozygous splice site mutation in KIAA0586 (alias TALPID3), a known lethal ciliopathy locus in model organisms.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on genetic analysis performed by the authors.

claim: KIAA0586 is a known lethal ciliopathy locus in model organisms.
source: By homozygosity mapping and whole-exome sequencing, we identified a novel locus, JBTS23, with a homozygous splice site mutation in KIAA0586 (alias TALPID3), a known lethal ciliopathy locus in model organisms.
evidence: This statement draws from established knowledge about KIAA0586 function in model organisms.

claim: Truncating KIAA0586 mutations were identified in two additional patients with JBTS.
source: Truncating KIAA0586 mutations were identified in two additional patients with JBTS.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on genetic analysis of patient samples.

claim: The mutation c.428delG (p.Arg143Lysfs*4) is unexpectedly common in the general population.
source: One mutation, c.428delG (p.Arg143Lysfs*4), is unexpectedly common in the general population and may be a major contributor to JBTS.
evidence: This is based on data from population databases and the authors' analysis.

claim: The mutation c.428delG (p.Arg143Lysfs*4) may be a major contributor to JBTS.
source: One mutation, c.428delG (p.Arg143Lysfs*4), is unexpectedly common in the general population and may be a major contributor to JBTS.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the frequency of the mutation and its presence in patients.

claim: KIAA0586 protein localizes at the basal body in human and mouse photoreceptors.
source: We demonstrate KIAA0586 protein localization at the basal body in human and mouse photoreceptors, as is common for JBTS proteins, and also in pericentriolar locations.
evidence: This is a primary finding demonstrated through immunofluorescence and immunoelectron microscopy experiments.

claim: KIAA0586 protein localizes in pericentriolar locations.
source: We demonstrate KIAA0586 protein localization at the basal body in human and mouse photoreceptors, as is common for JBTS proteins, and also in pericentriolar locations.
evidence: This is a primary finding demonstrated through immunofluorescence and immunoelectron microscopy experiments.

claim: Loss of TALPID3 (KIAA0586) function in animal models causes abnormal tissue polarity.
source: We show that loss of TALPID3 (KIAA0586) function in animal models causes abnormal tissue polarity, centrosome length and orientation, and centriolar satellites.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on experiments in chicken and mouse models.

claim: Loss of TALPID3 (KIAA0586) function in animal models causes abnormal centrosome length and orientation.
source: We show that loss of TALPID3 (KIAA0586) function in animal models causes abnormal tissue polarity, centrosome length and orientation, and centriolar satellites.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on experiments in chicken and mouse models.

claim: Loss of TALPID3 (KIAA0586) function in animal models causes abnormal centriolar satellites.
source: We show that loss of TALPID3 (KIAA0586) function in animal models causes abnormal tissue polarity, centrosome length and orientation, and centriolar satellites.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on experiments in chicken and mouse models.

claim: JBTS and other ciliopathies may in part result from cell polarity defects.
source: We propose that JBTS and other ciliopathies may in part result from cell polarity defects.
evidence: This is a speculative proposal based on the findings of the study.

claim: JBTS is a rare ciliopathy characterized by a specific midhindbrain malformation presenting as 'molar tooth sign' on axial MRI.
source: Joubert syndrome (JBTS) is a rare ciliopathy characterized by a specific midhindbrain malformation presenting as 'molar tooth sign' on axial MRI.
evidence: This is a definitional statement based on established clinical knowledge about JBTS.

claim: JBTS patients typically have a perturbed respiratory pattern in the neonatal period.
source: Patients typically have a perturbed respiratory pattern in the neonatal period and pronounced psychomotor delay.
evidence: This is based on established clinical knowledge about JBTS symptoms.

claim: JBTS patients typically have pronounced psychomotor delay.
source: Patients typically have a perturbed respiratory pattern in the neonatal period and pronounced psychomotor delay.
evidence: This is based on established clinical knowledge about JBTS symptoms.

claim: Depending on the genetic subtype, JBTS may have additional retinal degeneration, nephronophthisis, liver fibrosis, and skeletal abnormalities (such as polydactyly).
source: Depending on the genetic subtype, there may be additional retinal degeneration, nephronophthisis, liver fibrosis, and skeletal abnormalities (such as polydactyly).
evidence: This is based on established clinical knowledge about JBTS and is supported by citations.

claim: JBTS is genetically heterogeneous, with recessive mutations reported in more than 20 genes encoding proteins related to the function of cilia and associated structures.
source: JBTS is genetically heterogeneous, with recessive mutations reported in more than 20 genes encoding proteins related to the function of cilia and associated structures (Romani et al., 2013; Bachmann-Gagescu et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Cilia are axoneme-based organelles which protrude into the extracellular milieu, anchored to the cell by a modified centriole (basal body).
source: Cilia are axoneme-based organelles which protrude into the extracellular milieu, anchored to the cell by a modified centriole (basal body).
evidence: This is a definitional statement based on established knowledge about cilia structure.

claim: Cilia are present in virtually every cell type.
source: They are present in virtually every cell type (Christensen et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Non-motile 'primary' cilia play essential roles in mechanotransduction, chemosensation, and intracellular signal transduction.
source: Non-motile 'primary' cilia play essential roles in mechanotransduction, chemosensation, and intracellular signal transduction, including Hedgehog (Hh), PDGFα, and WNT pathways, in embryonic development and adult tissue homeostasis (Goetz and Anderson, 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Primary cilia are involved in Hedgehog (Hh), PDGFα, and WNT pathways in embryonic development and adult tissue homeostasis.
source: Non-motile 'primary' cilia play essential roles in mechanotransduction, chemosensation, and intracellular signal transduction, including Hedgehog (Hh), PDGFα, and WNT pathways, in embryonic development and adult tissue homeostasis (Goetz and Anderson, 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Highly modified and specialized cilia constitute the light-sensitive outer segments of retinal photoreceptor cells.
source: In addition, highly modified and specialized cilia constitute the light-sensitive outer segments of retinal photoreceptor cells.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about photoreceptor cell structure.

claim: Dysfunction of cilia, centrioles of basal bodies, and centrosomes can lead to a spectrum of developmental single- or multi-organ disorders termed 'ciliopathies'.
source: Dysfunction of cilia, centrioles of basal bodies, and centrosomes can lead to a spectrum of developmental single- or multi-organ disorders termed 'ciliopathies' (Bettencourt-Dias et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: KIAA0586 (TALPID3) is essential for vertebrate development and ciliogenesis.
source: KIAA0586 (TALPID3; MIM #610178, MIM #000979-9031) is essential for vertebrate development and ciliogenesis.
evidence: This statement is based on established knowledge from previous studies.

claim: The KIAA0586 (TALPID3) protein is localized at the centrosome in human, chicken, mouse, and zebrafish cells.
source: The KIAA0586 (TALPID3) protein is localized at the centrosome in human, chicken, mouse, and zebrafish cells (Yin et al., 2009; Ben et al., 2011; Wu et al., 2014), and in particular, at the distal end of the mother centriole—the basal body of cilia (Kobayashi et al., 2014a).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: KIAA0586 (TALPID3) protein is localized at the distal end of the mother centriole—the basal body of cilia.
source: The KIAA0586 (TALPID3) protein is localized at the centrosome in human, chicken, mouse, and zebrafish cells (Yin et al., 2009; Ben et al., 2011; Wu et al., 2014), and in particular, at the distal end of the mother centriole—the basal body of cilia (Kobayashi et al., 2014a).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: In model organisms, KIAA0586 null mutations cause failure of basal body docking and loss of cilia, leading to early embryonic lethal phenotypes.
source: In model organisms, KIAA0586 null mutations cause failure of basal body docking and loss of cilia, leading to early embryonic lethal phenotypes (Davey et al., 2006; Bangs et al., 2011; Ben et al., 2011; Stephen et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: KIAA0586 (TALPID3) binding partners include PCM1, Cep120, and CP110.
source: KIAA0586 (TALPID3) binding partners include PCM1, Cep120, and CP110, which interact with a known JBTS protein, CEP290 (Tsang and Dynlacht, 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: PCM1, Cep120, and CP110 interact with a known JBTS protein, CEP290.
source: KIAA0586 (TALPID3) binding partners include PCM1, Cep120, and CP110, which interact with a known JBTS protein, CEP290 (Tsang and Dynlacht, 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Three JBTS families with loss-of-function mutations in KIAA0586 were identified.
source: Here, we report three JBTS families with loss-of-function mutations in KIAA0586.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on genetic analysis.

claim: TALPID3 (KIAA0586) is not only essential for transduction of Hedgehog signaling but plays an important role in centrosomal localization, orientation, and length.
source: Using animal models, we demonstrate that TALPID3 (KIAA0586) is not only essential for transduction of Hedgehog signaling but plays an important role in centrosomal localization, orientation, and length.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on experiments in animal models.

claim: TALPID3 (KIAA0586) plays a key role in cell and tissue polarity beyond its established requirement for ciliogenesis.
source: Finally, and beyond its established requirement for ciliogenesis, TALPID3 (KIAA0586) plays a key role in cell and tissue polarity.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on experiments in animal models.

claim: The diagnosis of JBTS was based on the presence of a molar tooth sign in all three families.
source: The diagnosis of JBTS was based on the presence of a molar tooth sign in all three families.
evidence: This is a clinical observation from the patient data.

claim: Family 1 is a consanguineous Kurdish family from northeast Syria.
source: Family 1 (Figure 1A) is a consanguineous Kurdish family from northeast Syria.
evidence: This is demographic information about the patient family.

claim: Patient MR026-01 had delayed motor and speech development with an IQ estimated to be between 50 and 70.
source: Motor and speech development in MR026-01 were delayed, and his IQ was estimated to be between 50 and 70.
evidence: This is clinical data from patient examination.

claim: Patient MR026-01 had severe myopia, scoliosis, brachydactyly, distinct facial characteristics, and recurrent febrile seizures.
source: Further symptoms were severe myopia, scoliosis, brachydactyly, distinct facial characteristics, and recurrent febrile seizures.
evidence: This is clinical data from patient examination.

claim: Patient MR026-01 had reduced height (108 cm, −2.6 SD), normal weight (22 kg, −0.27 SD), and increased head circumference (57 cm, +2.3 SD) at age 6 years and 10 months.
source: Height was reduced (108 cm, −2.6 SD), weight was normal (22 kg, −0.27 SD), and head circumference was increased (57 cm, +2.3 SD).
evidence: This is clinical measurement data from patient examination.

claim: Patient MR026-04 had not reached any milestones and was wheelchair-bound at the age of 7 years.
source: MR026-04 had not reached any milestones, and at the age of 7 years, she was wheelchair-bound.
evidence: This is clinical data from patient examination.

claim: Patient MR026-04 had cognitive abilities weaker than her brother, with an IQ estimated to be below 35.
source: Cognitive abilities were weaker than in her brother, with an IQ estimated to be below 35.
evidence: This is clinical data from patient examination.

claim: Patient MR026-04 had severe muscular hypotonia, prolonged and therapy-resistant seizures since the age of 14 months, and hypothyroidism.
source: MR026-04 had similar physical characteristics as her brother, severe muscular hypotonia, prolonged and therapy-resistant seizures since the age of 14 months, and hypothyroidism.
evidence: This is clinical data from patient examination.

claim: Patient MR026-04 had height of 91 cm (1 SD), weight of 11.5 kg (−0.7 SD), and macrocephaly (head circumference of 59 cm, +8 SD) at the time of examination.
source: At the time of examination, her height was 91 cm (1 SD), weight was 11.5 kg (−0.7 SD), and there was macrocephaly (head circumference of 59 cm, +8 SD).
evidence: This is clinical measurement data from patient examination.

claim: Homozygosity mapping in Family 1 yielded eight homozygous chromosomal candidate regions.
source: Homozygosity mapping yielded eight homozygous chromosomal candidate regions (not shown), including the JBTS23 locus comprising KIAA0586.
evidence: This is a result from genetic analysis of Family 1.

claim: Patients MR026-01 and MR026-04 carry a homozygous splice site mutation, c.2414-1G>C.
source: Patients MR026-01 and MR026-04 carry a homozygous splice site mutation, c.2414-1G>C.
evidence: This is a result from genetic sequencing of the patients.

claim: Patient MD1 of Family 2 is compound heterozygous for two truncating mutations, including the prevalent c.428delG (p.Arg143Lysfs*4) allele.
source: Patient MD1 of Family 2 is compound heterozygous for two truncating mutations, including the prevalent c.428delG (p.Arg143Lysfs*4) allele.
evidence: This is a result from genetic sequencing of the patient.

claim: Patient G2 is double heterozygous for c.428delG in KIAA0586, and a frameshift mutation in KIF7 (JBTS12; c.811delG, p.Glu271Argfs*51).
source: Patient G2 is double heterozygous for c.428delG in KIAA0586, and a frameshift mutation in KIF7 (JBTS12; c.811delG, p.Glu271Argfs*51).
evidence: This is a result from genetic sequencing of the patient.

claim: Patient G2 carries three potentially pathogenic variants in the ciliopathy genes CEP41, KIF14, and WDPCP.
source: He also carries three potentially pathogenic variants in the ciliopathy genes CEP41, KIF14, and WDPCP (blue).
evidence: This is a result from genetic sequencing of the patient.

claim: The c.2414-1G>C mutation causes aberrant transcripts due to usage of alternative exonic acceptor splice sites and skipping of exon 18.
source: The gel electrophoresis shows the aberrant transcripts due to c.2414-1G>C.
evidence: This is demonstrated by RT-PCR and gel electrophoresis data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The third coiled-coil domain in human KIAA0586 is the counterpart of the functionally essential fourth coiled-coil domain in chicken.
source: The third coiled-coil domain is the counterpart of the functionally essential fourth coiled-coil domain in chicken (framed in red).
evidence: This is based on sequence comparison and functional knowledge from previous studies.

claim: Chicken TALPID3 (KIAA0586) is highly similar to the human protein.
source: Chicken TALPID3 (KIAA0586) is highly similar to the human protein.
evidence: This is based on sequence comparison shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The talpid3 mutation in chicken results in an early frameshift and loss of three coiled-coil domains, including the fourth one.
source: The talpid3 mutation results in an early frameshift and loss of three coiled-coil domains, including the fourth one.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Biallelic KIF7 mutations cause JBTS type 12 in human.
source: Biallelic KIF7 mutations cause JBTS type 12 in human (Dafinger et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Overexpression of IFT57 does not have an effect on patterning of the neural tube in the talpid3 chicken.
source: Overexpression of IFT57 does not have an effect on patterning of the neural tube in the talpid3 chicken.
evidence: This is demonstrated by in ovo complementation experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Overexpression of KIF7 does not rescue or alter neural tube patterning in the talpid3 chicken.
source: Overexpression of KIF7 does not rescue or alter neural tube patterning in the talpid3 chicken.
evidence: This is demonstrated by in ovo complementation experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: siRNA knockdown of KIF7 resulted in a weak dorsalization of PAX7 but no expansion of ISLET1.
source: siRNA knockdown of KIF7 resulted in a weak dorsalization of PAX7 but no expansion of ISLET1.
evidence: This is demonstrated by siRNA experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Talpid3+/− Kif7+/− mice showed no gross anatomical abnormalities.
source: Talpid3+/− Kif7+/− mice showed no gross anatomical abnormalities, neither were developmental brain defects identified through MRI (D) or histology (E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by examination of double heterozygous mice shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D,E.

claim: No abnormalities were identified in either the percentage of ciliated cells or the length of cilia in MEFs derived from Talpid3+/− Kif7+/− mice.
source: No abnormalities were identified in either the percentage of ciliated cells (F), nor the length of cilia (G) in MEFs derived from wildtype, Talpid3+/+Kif7+/−, Talpid3+/− Kif7+/+ or Talpid3+/− Kif7+/− mice.
evidence: This is demonstrated by analysis of MEFs shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F,G.

claim: KIAA0586 (TALPID3) and KIF7 do not act epistatically.
source: We conclude that KIAA0586 (TALPID3) and KIF7 do not act epistatically and hypothesize that additional genetic alterations in ciliopathy genes of patient G2, eventually including those identified in CEP41 (JBTS15), KIF14, and WDPCP, may contribute to a mutational load that is sufficient to elicit a JBTS phenotype on a KIAA0586+/−; KIF7+/− background.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the experiments with double heterozygous mice and chicken.

claim: Additional genetic alterations in ciliopathy genes of patient G2 may contribute to a mutational load that is sufficient to elicit a JBTS phenotype on a KIAA0586+/−; KIF7+/− background.
source: We conclude that KIAA0586 (TALPID3) and KIF7 do not act epistatically and hypothesize that additional genetic alterations in ciliopathy genes of patient G2, eventually including those identified in CEP41 (JBTS15), KIF14, and WDPCP, may contribute to a mutational load that is sufficient to elicit a JBTS phenotype on a KIAA0586+/−; KIF7+/− background.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the genetic findings in patient G2.

claim: Patient MD1 was born at 34 3/7 weeks gestation following preterm premature rupture of membranes at 26 weeks.
source: Patient MD1 was born at 34 3/7 weeks gestation following preterm premature rupture of membranes at 26 weeks.
evidence: This is clinical data from the patient's medical history.

claim: At birth, patient MD1 was found to have cardiac defects including a patent ductus arteriosus (PDA), patent foramen ovale (PFO) and a 3/6 ventricular septal defect (VSD) causing persistent pulmonary hypertension 24 hr after birth.
source: At birth, patient MD1 was found to have cardiac defects including a patent ductus arteriosus (PDA), patent foramen ovale (PFO) and a 3/6 ventricular septal defect (VSD) causing persistent pulmonary hypertension 24 hr after birth.
evidence: This is clinical data from patient examination.

claim: At 7 months, patient MD1 was found to have a superior vena cava duplication.
source: At 7 months, MD1 was found to have a superior vena cava duplication.
evidence: This is clinical data from patient examination.

claim: At 2 years of age, patient MD1 had hypotonia which inhibited motor actions, although she crawled proficiently, used sign language and single words, and self-fed by hand and with utensils.
source: At 2 years of age, MD1 had hypotonia which inhibited motor actions, although she crawled proficiently, used sign language and single words, and self-fed by hand and with utensils.
evidence: This is clinical data from patient examination.

claim: Patient MD1 had type I bilateral Duane syndrome with no abduction in either eye, narrowing of the palprebal fissure of the inturned eye, was farsighted, had thin tooth enamel, held her jaw sideways in a cross-bite pattern, and had long fingers with a slight clinodactyly of the fifth finger.
source: In addition, she had type I bilateral Duane syndrome with no abduction in either eye, narrowing of the palprebal fissure of the inturned eye, was farsighted, had thin tooth enamel, held her jaw sideways in a cross-bite pattern, and had long fingers with a slight clinodactyly of the fifth finger.
evidence: This is clinical data from patient examination.

claim: Patient MD1 had a broad forehead, arched eyebrows, ptosis of the right eye, and a triangle-shaped mouth.
source: She had a broad forehead, arched eyebrows, ptosis of the right eye, and a triangle-shaped mouth.
evidence: This is clinical data from patient examination.

claim: Patient MD1 had intermittent hyperpnea/apnea during awake periods.
source: There was intermittent hyperpnea/apnea during awake periods.
evidence: This is clinical data from patient examination.

claim: Patient MD1 had no liver, kidney, or eye abnormalities at 2 years of age.
source: Patient MD1 had no liver, kidney, or eye abnormalities at 2 years of age.
evidence: This is clinical data from patient examination.

claim: Patient G2 displayed a relatively mild JBTS phenotype with developmental delay and behavioral abnormalities, but no dysmorphic signs and no renal, retinal, skeletal, or liver abnormalities.
source: Family 3 (Figure 1C) is of German origin: patient G2 displayed a relatively mild JBTS phenotype with developmental delay and behavioral abnormalities, but no dysmorphic signs and no renal, retinal, skeletal, or liver abnormalities.
evidence: This is clinical data from patient examination.

claim: Genome-wide SNP genotyping in Family 1 identified eight homozygous chromosomal candidate regions with a total range of 67.1 Mb.
source: Genome-wide SNP genotyping in Family 1 identified eight homozygous chromosomal candidate regions with a total range of 67.1 Mb.
evidence: This is a result from genetic analysis of Family 1.

claim: By WES, the homozygous mutation c.2414-1G>C in intron 17, affecting the invariant consensus of the exon 18 acceptor splice site, was found in the index patient, MR026-01, and his affected sister, MR026-04.
source: By WES, the homozygous mutation c.2414-1G>C in intron 17, affecting the invariant consensus of the exon 18 acceptor splice site, was found in the index patient, MR026-01, and his affected sister, MR026-04.
evidence: This is a result from whole-exome sequencing of the patients.

claim: Segregation analysis in Family 1 was compatible with causality.
source: Segregation analysis in the family was compatible with causality (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is based on genetic analysis of the family pedigree.

claim: The c.2414-1G>C mutation was absent from 372 healthy Syrian controls, including 92 of Kurdish origin.
source: The mutation was absent from 372 healthy Syrian controls, including 92 of Kurdish origin, and not listed in the ExAC database.
evidence: This is based on screening of control populations.

claim: The c.2414-1G>C mutation was not listed in the ExAC database.
source: The mutation was absent from 372 healthy Syrian controls, including 92 of Kurdish origin, and not listed in the ExAC database.
evidence: This is based on database searches.

claim: In patient MD1 from Family 2, WES identified compound heterozygosity for the KIAA0586 mutations c.428delG (p.Arg143Lysfs*4) and c.2512C>T (p.Arg838*), each inherited from a healthy parent.
source: In patient MD1 from Family 2, WES identified compound heterozygosity for the KIAA0586 mutations c.428delG (p.Arg143Lysfs*4; rs534542684; MAF of 0.39% in ExAC db) and c.2512C>T (p.Arg838*), each inherited from a healthy parent (Figure 1B), and both resulting in premature stop codons.
evidence: This is a result from whole-exome sequencing of the patient and parents.

claim: The c.428delG mutation has a MAF of 0.39% in the ExAC database.
source: In patient MD1 from Family 2, WES identified compound heterozygosity for the KIAA0586 mutations c.428delG (p.Arg143Lysfs*4; rs534542684; MAF of 0.39% in ExAC db) and c.2512C>T (p.Arg838*), each inherited from a healthy parent (Figure 1B), and both resulting in premature stop codons.
evidence: This is based on database searches.

claim: Both c.428delG and c.2512C>T mutations result in premature stop codons.
source: In patient MD1 from Family 2, WES identified compound heterozygosity for the KIAA0586 mutations c.428delG (p.Arg143Lysfs*4; rs534542684; MAF of 0.39% in ExAC db) and c.2512C>T (p.Arg838*), each inherited from a healthy parent (Figure 1B), and both resulting in premature stop codons.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and prediction of protein consequences.

claim: The coiled-coil domain (residues 531–571 in human KIAA0586) is essential for KIAA0586 function in mouse, chicken, and zebrafish.
source: Because the coiled-coil domain, which is essential for KIAA0586 function in mouse, chicken, and zebrafish (residues 531–571 and residues 497–530 in human and chicken KIAA0586 (TALPID3), respectively; Figure 1F), would be lost in a truncated protein derived from the c.428delG mutation, we consider it a loss-of-function mutation (as is the case for the talpid3 chicken mutation which introduces a frameshift 3′ to c.428 in the chicken ortholog, Figure 1F).
evidence: This is based on previous functional studies in model organisms.

claim: The c.428delG mutation is considered a loss-of-function mutation because the essential coiled-coil domain would be lost in a truncated protein.
source: Because the coiled-coil domain, which is essential for KIAA0586 function in mouse, chicken, and zebrafish (residues 531–571 and residues 497–530 in human and chicken KIAA0586 (TALPID3), respectively; Figure 1F), would be lost in a truncated protein derived from the c.428delG mutation, we consider it a loss-of-function mutation (as is the case for the talpid3 chicken mutation which introduces a frameshift 3′ to c.428 in the chicken ortholog, Figure 1F).
evidence: This is an inference based on the predicted protein structure and comparison to known loss-of-function mutations.

claim: The c.428delG mutation is clearly recessive because the father of the patient is a healthy carrier.
source: Like the Talpid3/TALPID3 null mutations in mouse and chicken, c.428delG is clearly recessive because the father of the patient is a healthy carrier.
evidence: This is based on observation of the carrier parent's phenotype.

claim: The c.2512C>T (p.Arg838*) mutation is predicted to lead to nonsense-mediated decay (NMD) or a truncated protein, but with preservation of the essential coiled-coil domain.
source: The c.2512C>T (p.Arg838*) mutation is predicted to lead to nonsense-mediated decay (NMD) or a truncated protein, but with preservation of the essential coiled-coil domain.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the location of the mutation and knowledge of NMD mechanisms.

claim: Patient G2 was a known carrier of a heterozygous N-terminal frameshift mutation in exon 3 of the JBTS12 gene KIF7, c.811delG (p.Glu271Argfs*51).
source: The simplex patient of Family 3, G2, was a known carrier of a heterozygous N-terminal frameshift mutation in exon 3 of the JBTS12 gene KIF7, c.811delG (p.Glu271Argfs*51) (Dafinger et al., 2011).
evidence: This is based on previous genetic analysis reported in a cited study.

claim: WES of Family 3 trio additionally identified the c.428delG (p.Arg143Lysfs*4) mutation in KIAA0586 in patient G2.
source: WES of the family trio (patient G2 and his parents) additionally identified the c.428delG (p.Arg143Lysfs*4) mutation in KIAA0586, in the patient (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a result from whole-exome sequencing of the patient and parents.

claim: Disease in patient G2 could be due to biallelic mutations either in KIF7 (JBTS12) or in KIAA0586 (JBTS23), assuming that the 'missing mutation' has escaped detection by sequencing due to an extra-exonic localization.
source: We hypothesized that disease in patient G2 could be due to biallelic mutations either in KIF7 (JBTS12) or in KIAA0586 (JBTS23), assuming that the 'missing mutation' has escaped detection by sequencing due to an extra-exonic localization.
evidence: This is a hypothesis to explain the genetic findings in patient G2.

claim: Genome-wide CGH did not reveal structural alterations adjacent to or within KIF7 or KIAA0586 in patient G2.
source: Genome-wide CGH (Affymetrix 6.0 SNP array) did not reveal structural alterations adjacent to or within KIF7 (Dafinger et al., 2011) or KIAA0586, thereby largely excluding a large deletion or duplication.
evidence: This is a result from genome-wide copy number analysis.

claim: PCR amplification and sequencing of KIAA0586 exons from cDNA did not reveal aberrant splicing in patient G2.
source: PCR amplification and subsequent sequencing of KIAA0586 exons from cDNA did not reveal aberrant splicing as a potential hint for a deep intronic splice site mutation.
evidence: This is a result from RT-PCR analysis.

claim: KIF7 and KIAA0586 both encode modulators of GLI processing.
source: Because KIF7 and KIAA0586 both encode modulators of GLI processing and c.428delGKIAA0586 and c.811delGKIF7 likely represent recessive loss-of-function mutations, we investigated the possibility of a potential epistatic effect predisposing to JBTS.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about the function of these proteins.

claim: No epistatic interactions between KIAA0586 and KIF7 were identified in mouse and chicken experiments.
source: No such interactions were identified in mouse and chicken experiments (details are fully described in Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experiments described in the supplement.

claim: Unidentified mutations are likely to be involved in patient G2, either mutations in KIF7, KIAA0586 or biallelic mutations in another (yet unknown) JBTS gene.
source: Therefore, unidentified mutations are likely to be involved, either mutations in KIF7, KIAA0586 (e.g., deep intronic mutations or alterations in non-coding regulatory regions which would both not be covered by WES) or biallelic mutations in another (yet unknown) JBTS gene.
evidence: This is a hypothesis to explain the genetic findings in patient G2.

claim: WES revealed heterozygous missense variants in three known recessive ciliopathy genes in patient G2: CEP41, KIF14, and WDPCP.
source: WES revealed further heterozygous missense variants in three known recessive ciliopathy genes in patient G2 (Figure 1C), all affecting evolutionarily conserved residues of the respective proteins: (1) c.536 G>A (p.Arg179His, rs140259402; MAF of 0.001647% in ExAC db) in CEP41, the gene associated with JBTS15 (Lee et al., 2012). (2) c.3181A>G (p.Ile1061Val; MAF of 0.01155% in ExAC db) in KIF14, a gene associated with a lethal fetal ciliopathy phenotype (Filges et al., 2014). (3) c.1333G>C (p.Ala445Pro, rs61734466; MAF of 0.6609% in ExAC db) in WDPCP, the gene associated with Bardet–Biedl syndrome type 15 (BBS15), and a putative contributor to Meckel Gruber syndrome (Kim et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a result from whole-exome sequencing of patient G2.

claim: All three variants in CEP41, KIF14, and WDPCP were of paternal origin in patient G2.
source: All variants were of paternal origin and rare in the general population except the WDPCP allele, which had been maternally inherited and which has been annotated homozygously in five healthy individuals (ExAC db), indicating that this is a benign variant.
evidence: This is based on segregation analysis in the family.

claim: The WDPCP variant c.1333G>C (p.Ala445Pro) is likely a benign variant because it has been annotated homozygously in five healthy individuals.
source: All variants were of paternal origin and rare in the general population except the WDPCP allele, which had been maternally inherited and which has been annotated homozygously in five healthy individuals (ExAC db), indicating that this is a benign variant.
evidence: This is an inference based on population database data.

claim: Genome-wide CGH did not show structural alterations adjacent to or within CEP41, KIF14, or WDPCP in patient G2.
source: Genome-wide CGH (Affymetrix 6.0 SNP array) did not show structural alterations adjacent to or within CEP41, KIF14, or WDPCP.
evidence: This is a result from genome-wide copy number analysis.

claim: A paternally inherited frameshift variant, c.206_207insA (p.Ser70Valfs*3), in PLA2G3 was identified in patient G2.
source: In addition, we searched the WES data of patient G2 for heterozygous putative loss-of-function (that is, truncating) variants in genes with documented ciliary function. This revealed a paternally inherited frameshift variant, c.206_207insA (p.Ser70Valfs*3), in PLA2G3, the gene encoding phospholipase A2.
evidence: This is a result from whole-exome sequencing analysis.

claim: PLA2G3 was found to be a negative regulator of ciliogenesis and ciliary membrane protein targeting in a functional genomic screen.
source: In a functional genomic screen, PLA2G3 was found to be a negative regulator of ciliogenesis and ciliary membrane protein targeting (Kim et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The p.Ser70Valfs*3 PLA2G3 variant is relatively common (MAF of 0.4060 in ExAC db), but has not been documented in homozygous state in healthy individuals.
source: The p.Ser70Valfs*3PLA2G3 variant is relatively common, but has not been documented in homozygous state in healthy individuals (MAF of 0.4060 in ExAC db).
evidence: This is based on population database data.

claim: The c.2414-1G>C mutation affects the invariant consensus of the acceptor splice site of exon 18.
source: The c.2414-1G>C mutation affects the invariant consensus of the acceptor splice site of exon 18.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis of the mutation.

claim: RT-PCR and Sanger sequencing revealed three aberrant splicing products due to the c.2414-1G>C mutation.
source: RT-PCR and Sanger sequencing of the fragments amplified from cDNA revealed three aberrant splicing products due to usage of alternative exonic acceptor splice sites at AG motifs within exon 18 and due to skipping of exon 18 (Figure 1D,E): a 13-bp deletion that results in a premature termination codon (alternative acceptor splice site at c.2425/2426AG), a 108-bp in-frame deletion (alternative acceptor splice site at c.2520/2521AG), and a 188-bp deletion due to skipping of exon 18 that results in a premature stop codon.
evidence: This is a result from RT-PCR and sequencing analysis.

claim: The aberrant transcripts due to c.2414-1G>C were present in the cDNA from both patients MR026-01 and MR026-04, but not in the cDNA of a healthy control individual.
source: These aberrant transcripts were present in the cDNA from both patients, but not in the cDNA of a healthy control individual (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a result from RT-PCR analysis comparing patients and controls.

claim: The mutant mRNA molecules from c.2414-1G>C are likely to be degraded by NMD.
source: The mutant mRNA molecules are likely to be degraded by NMD.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the presence of premature stop codons.

claim: If the mutant transcripts from c.2414-1G>C were stable, the essential coiled-coil domain would be preserved.
source: If the mutant transcripts were stable, the essential coiled-coil domain (Figure 1E), which mediates centrosomal localization and function of KIAA0586 protein (Yin et al., 2009; Wu et al., 2014), would be preserved.
evidence: This is a conditional inference based on the location of the mutation and protein structure.

claim: KIAA0586 (Talpid3) is a centrosomal protein and localizes to the basal body and the adjacent centriole of primary cilia in human RPE1 and IMCD3 cells.
source: KIAA0586 (Talpid3) is a centrosomal protein and localizes to the basal body and the adjacent centriole of primary cilia in human RPE1, IMCD3 cells (Figure 2A), and other cell types (Kobayashi et al., 2014a; Wu et al., 2014).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence shown in Figure 2A and supported by citations.

claim: Immunofluorescence analysis of the retina of wildtype C57BL/6 mice showed Talpid3 expression in the photoreceptor layer, the outer and inner plexiform layer, and the ganglion cell layer.
source: Immunofluorescence analysis of the retina of wildtype C57BL/6 mice allowed us to allocate Talpid3 expression to different retinal layers, namely the photoreceptor layer, the outer and inner plexiform layer, and the ganglion cell layer (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Co-staining with centrin-3 demonstrated Talpid3/KIAA0586 localization in the ciliary region at the joint between the inner and outer segment of photoreceptor cells in mouse and human retina.
source: Co-staining with the ciliary marker centrin-3 (Trojan et al., 2008) demonstrated Talpid3/KIAA0586 localization in the ciliary region at the joint between the inner and outer segment of photoreceptor cells in cryosections through the mouse retina and the retina of a human donor eye (Figure 2B,C,E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence shown in Figure 2B,C,E.

claim: Talpid3/KIAA0586 specifically localized at the basal body (mother centriole) and the adjacent centriole as well as between the two centrioles, but not in the connecting cilium of mouse and human photoreceptor cells.
source: Higher magnification revealed that Talpid3/KIAA0586 specifically localized at the basal body (mother centriole) and the adjacent centriole as well as between the two centrioles, but not in the connecting cilium of mouse and human photoreceptor cells (Figure 2D,F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by high magnification immunofluorescence shown in Figure 2D,F.

claim: Immunoelectron microscopy of mouse photoreceptor cilia confirmed Talpid3 labeling at centrioles and in the pericentriolar region in the apical inner segment of photoreceptor cells.
source: These findings were confirmed by immunoelectron microscopy of Talpid3 labeling on sections through mouse photoreceptor cilia (Figure 2G,H). Immunostaining was found at centrioles and in the pericentriolar region in the apical inner segment of photoreceptor cells.
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoelectron microscopy shown in Figure 2G,H.

claim: The talpid3/Talpid3−/− phenotype in model animals has been attributed to the role of TALPID3 in ciliogenesis and the subsequent loss of Hh-dependent patterning.
source: The talpid3/Talpid3−/− phenotype in model animals has thus far been attributed to the role of TALPID3 in ciliogenesis and the subsequent loss of Hh-dependent patterning.
evidence: This is based on previous interpretations of the phenotype in model organisms.

claim: The patients in this study did not display any overt defects typical for impaired Hh signaling such as polydactyly or hypotelorism.
source: However, the patients in this study did not display any overt defects typical for impaired Hh signaling such as polydactyly or hypotelorism, which have been described in other patients with JBTS (Bachmann-Gagescu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on clinical examination of the patients.

claim: Talpid3 chicken embryos have polycystic kidneys.
source: Talpid3 chicken embryos also have polycystic kidneys (Yin et al., 2009), a phenotype that is frequently ascribed to a loss of oriented cell division (Happe et al., 2011; Carroll and Yu, 2012), as well as cell migration defects (Bangs et al., 2011), which may also occur due to loss of cell polarity (Happe et al., 2011; Carroll and Yu, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Polycystic kidneys are frequently ascribed to a loss of oriented cell division.
source: Talpid3 chicken embryos also have polycystic kidneys (Yin et al., 2009), a phenotype that is frequently ascribed to a loss of oriented cell division (Happe et al., 2011; Carroll and Yu, 2012), as well as cell migration defects (Bangs et al., 2011), which may also occur due to loss of cell polarity (Happe et al., 2011; Carroll and Yu, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Talpid3 chicken embryos have cell migration defects.
source: Talpid3 chicken embryos also have polycystic kidneys (Yin et al., 2009), a phenotype that is frequently ascribed to a loss of oriented cell division (Happe et al., 2011; Carroll and Yu, 2012), as well as cell migration defects (Bangs et al., 2011), which may also occur due to loss of cell polarity (Happe et al., 2011; Carroll and Yu, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: At E10, embryonic chicken feather buds express β-catenin in an oriented manner, with a larger domain in the anterior part of the bud.
source: At E10, embryonic chicken feather buds express β-catenin in an oriented manner, with a larger domain in the anterior part of the bud (Figure 3A,C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in situ hybridization shown in Figure 3A,C.

claim: 88% of wildtype feather buds at E10 are oriented with β-catenin expression in the anterior part (n = 117/133).
source: While 88% of wildtype feather buds at E10 are oriented in this manner (n = 117/133), only 21% of stage-matched talpid3 feather buds were (n = 38/179).
evidence: This is quantification of data from in situ hybridization experiments.

claim: Only 21% of stage-matched talpid3 feather buds at E10 showed correct orientation of β-catenin expression (n = 38/179).
source: While 88% of wildtype feather buds at E10 are oriented in this manner (n = 117/133), only 21% of stage-matched talpid3 feather buds were (n = 38/179).
evidence: This is quantification of data from in situ hybridization experiments.

claim: 22% of talpid3 feather buds were oriented in the wrong direction (n = 39/179).
source: 22% of talpid3 buds were oriented in the wrong direction (n = 39/179) and 57% had failed to show any orientation of β-catenin expression (n = 102/179; Figure 3C′).
evidence: This is quantification of data from in situ hybridization experiments.

claim: 57% of talpid3 feather buds had failed to show any orientation of β-catenin expression (n = 102/179).
source: 22% of talpid3 buds were oriented in the wrong direction (n = 39/179) and 57% had failed to show any orientation of β-catenin expression (n = 102/179; Figure 3C′).
evidence: This is quantification of data from in situ hybridization experiments.

claim: Talpid3 feather buds frequently merged (29% of buds).
source: Talpid3 feather buds also frequently merged (29% of buds; asterisk, Figure 3B′′).
evidence: This is quantification of observations from in situ hybridization experiments.

claim: The skin of talpid3 embryos did not show the characteristic rostral-caudal polarization of wildtype skin.
source: Thus, the skin of talpid3 embryos did not show the characteristic rostral-caudal polarization of wildtype skin.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the feather bud orientation data.

claim: The hair cells of the inner ear have a highly polarized structure determined by the non-canonical Wnt-PCP signaling pathway.
source: The hair cells (HCs) of the inner ear (known as the basilar papilla (BP) in chicken) have a highly polarized structure determined by the non-canonical Wnt-PCP signaling pathway.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about hair cell development.

claim: In wildtype chicken, individual hair cells exhibit an orientated actin-based stereocilia bundle, the apex of which lies at the abneural side of the cell, where within an actin-free 'bare zone', a single kinocilium forms.
source: In the wildtype chicken, as in mouse, individual HCs exhibit an orientated actin-based stereocilia bundle, the apex of which lies at the abneural side of the cell, where within an actin-free 'bare zone', a single kinocilium (a microtubule-based true cilium) forms (arrow, Figure 3D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by SEM and immunofluorescence shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The hair cells of talpid3 embryos formed actin filament bundles but no kinocilium.
source: The HCs of talpid3 embryos formed actin filament bundles (curved line, Figure 3E), but no kinocilium, demonstrating that, as with other tissues studied, loss of TALPID3 impairs ciliogenesis.
evidence: This is demonstrated by SEM shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Loss of TALPID3 impairs ciliogenesis in hair cells.
source: The HCs of talpid3 embryos formed actin filament bundles (curved line, Figure 3E), but no kinocilium, demonstrating that, as with other tissues studied, loss of TALPID3 impairs ciliogenesis.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observation that talpid3 hair cells lack kinocilia.

claim: Stereocilia bundles in talpid3 hair cells frequently lacked polarity compared to wildtype hair cells (talpid3 n = 1086/1195; wt n = 258/502).
source: Furthermore, although stereocilia were present in talpid3 HCs, stereocilia bundles frequently lacked polarity compared to wildtype HCs as indicated by either centrally located stereocilia bundles in SEM or actin filaments throughout the cell (talpid3 n = 1086/1195; wt n = 258/502; Figure 3D–G,L).
evidence: This is quantification of observations from SEM and immunofluorescence experiments.

claim: Orientation of the polarized stereocilia bundles that did form in talpid3 hair cells was abnormal.
source: Orientation of the polarized stereocilia bundles that did form in talpid3 HCs was also abnormal (Figure 3E,G,N).
evidence: This is demonstrated by analysis of stereocilia orientation shown in Figure 3E,G,N.

claim: Talpid3 hair cells showed disrupted polarity.
source: Thus, talpid3 HCs showed disrupted polarity.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the stereocilia orientation and localization data.

claim: Loss of TALPID3 function prevents basal body docking.
source: Loss of TALPID3 function prevents basal body docking (Yin et al., 2009), which we have previously suggested to be due to failure of centrosome migration (Stephen et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Failure of basal body docking has been suggested to be due to failure of centrosome migration.
source: Loss of TALPID3 function prevents basal body docking (Yin et al., 2009), which we have previously suggested to be due to failure of centrosome migration (Stephen et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: The migration and subsequent localization and docking of the centriole is crucial to establish polarity and placement of the actin bundle in the hair cell.
source: The migration and subsequent localization and docking of the centriole is crucial to establish polarity and placement of the actin bundle in the HC (Tarchini et al., 2013), and we therefore hypothesized that disturbed cell polarity may result from defective centrosome migration in talpid3 HCs.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: 95% of wildtype hair cells exhibited a basal body (centrosome) within the abneural bare zone (n = 632 from 7 samples).
source: Using antibodies against γ tubulin to determine the localization of the centriole within the actin-negative abneural bare zone in the HCs, 95% of wildtype HCs exhibited a basal body (centrosome) within the abneural bare zone (n = 632 from 7 samples, Figure 3H,J,N).
evidence: This is quantification of immunofluorescence data.

claim: Only 49% of talpid3 hair cells exhibited a centriole within the bare zone (either abneural or abnormally polarized; n = 219 from 6 samples).
source: In contrast, only 49% of talpid3 cells exhibited a centriole within the bare zone (either abneural or abnormally polarized; n = 219 from 6 samples; Figure 3I,K,N), thus demonstrating that the intracellular organization of talpid3 cells was frequently abnormal.
evidence: This is quantification of immunofluorescence data.

claim: The intracellular organization of talpid3 hair cells was frequently abnormal.
source: In contrast, only 49% of talpid3 cells exhibited a centriole within the bare zone (either abneural or abnormally polarized; n = 219 from 6 samples; Figure 3I,K,N), thus demonstrating that the intracellular organization of talpid3 cells was frequently abnormal.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the centriole localization data.

claim: Centrioles were frequently observed on the neural side of talpid3 hair cells.
source: Furthermore, and in agreement with the failure of correct polarization of the stereocilia, centrioles were frequently observed on the neural side of talpid3 HCs (Figure 3Kii).
evidence: This is an observation from immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3Kii.

claim: Failure of centriolar migration in talpid3 cells results in abnormal cell polarization and stereocilia formation in hair cells.
source: We conclude that failure of centriolar migration in talpid3 cells results in abnormal cell polarization and stereocilia formation in HCs.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the hair cell data.

claim: 49% of talpid3 hair cells exhibited a centriole correctly localized yet ciliogenesis was completely disrupted, suggesting that the failure of ciliogenesis may not only be due to impaired centriolar migration.
source: Because 49% of talpid3 cells did exhibit a centriole correctly localized yet ciliogenesis was completely disrupted, the failure of ciliogenesis may not only be due to impaired centriolar migration.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that some talpid3 cells have correctly localized centrioles but still lack cilia.

claim: Directional cell migration is intimately linked to the localization of the centrosome between the leading edge of the migrating cell and the Golgi apparatus.
source: Directional cell migration is also intimately linked to the localization of the centrosome between the leading edge of the migrating cell and the Golgi apparatus.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about cell migration.

claim: Talpid3−/− MEFs show abnormal cell migration.
source: Talpid3−/− MEFs show abnormal cell migration (Bangs et al., 2011), and we therefore examined if the orientation of the Golgi apparatus to the leading edge of migrating cells was also disrupted by a loss of Talpid3 function in mouse, in an in vitro scratch assay (Figure 3O,P).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The angle of orientation was within 40° in 69% of wildtype cells and 55% of Talpid3−/− cells in a scratch assay.
source: The angle of orientation was within 40° in 69% of wildtype cells and 55% of Talpid3−/− cells, whilst 20% of Talpid3−/− cells exhibited orientation angles greater than 60° compared to 11% of wildtype cells (Figure 3Q′; wildtype cells = 132, Talpid3−/− cells = 117 from two experiments; Figure 3O–Q), suggesting a reduction in intracellular polarization of the Golgi apparatus to the leading edge in the Talpid3−/− MEFs (Figure 3O,P).
evidence: This is quantification of data from scratch assay experiments.

claim: 20% of Talpid3−/− cells exhibited orientation angles greater than 60° compared to 11% of wildtype cells in a scratch assay.
source: The angle of orientation was within 40° in 69% of wildtype cells and 55% of Talpid3−/− cells, whilst 20% of Talpid3−/− cells exhibited orientation angles greater than 60° compared to 11% of wildtype cells (Figure 3Q′; wildtype cells = 132, Talpid3−/− cells = 117 from two experiments; Figure 3O–Q), suggesting a reduction in intracellular polarization of the Golgi apparatus to the leading edge in the Talpid3−/− MEFs (Figure 3O,P).
evidence: This is quantification of data from scratch assay experiments.

claim: There is a reduction in intracellular polarization of the Golgi apparatus to the leading edge in Talpid3−/− MEFs.
source: The angle of orientation was within 40° in 69% of wildtype cells and 55% of Talpid3−/− cells, whilst 20% of Talpid3−/− cells exhibited orientation angles greater than 60° compared to 11% of wildtype cells (Figure 3Q′; wildtype cells = 132, Talpid3−/− cells = 117 from two experiments; Figure 3O–Q), suggesting a reduction in intracellular polarization of the Golgi apparatus to the leading edge in the Talpid3−/− MEFs (Figure 3O,P).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the scratch assay data.

claim: KIAA0586 (TALPID3;Talpid3) plays an essential role in the internal organization and polarization of cells, likely through its action on the centrosome.
source: Thus, KIAA0586 (TALPID3;Talpid3) plays an essential role in the internal organization and polarization of cells, likely through its action on the centrosome.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the cell polarity data from multiple experiments.

claim: JBTS primarily affects the brain of the patients.
source: JBTS primarily affects the brain of the patients.
evidence: This is based on established clinical knowledge about JBTS.

claim: The choroid plexus is a highly polarized multiciliated neuroepithelium.
source: The choroid plexus is a highly polarized multiciliated neuroepithelium in which we have previously shown, as now in HCs, a failure of centrosome migration in talpid3 mutant chickens (Stephen et al., 2013).
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about choroid plexus structure.

claim: There is a failure of centrosome migration in the choroid plexus of talpid3 mutant chickens.
source: The choroid plexus is a highly polarized multiciliated neuroepithelium in which we have previously shown, as now in HCs, a failure of centrosome migration in talpid3 mutant chickens (Stephen et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: Wildtype choroid plexus cells exhibited a distinctive polarization with an apical, centriolar zone (CZ) above a separate zone of mitochondria (MZ).
source: Wildtype choroid plexus cells exhibited a distinctive polarization with an apical, centriolar zone (CZ, Figure 4A) above a separate zone of mitochondria (MZ, Figure 4A); the most apical mitochondria were found an average of 7 µm from the apical surface (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by electron microscopy shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The most apical mitochondria in wildtype choroid plexus cells were found an average of 7 µm from the apical surface.
source: Wildtype choroid plexus cells exhibited a distinctive polarization with an apical, centriolar zone (CZ, Figure 4A) above a separate zone of mitochondria (MZ, Figure 4A); the most apical mitochondria were found an average of 7 µm from the apical surface (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is quantification of electron microscopy measurements.

claim: The mitochondria in talpid3 choroid plexus are found in the most apical zone, an average of 3 µm from the apical surface.
source: In contrast, the mitochondria in talpid3 choroid plexus are found in the most apical zone, an average of 3 µm from the apical surface (m, Figure 4B), and centrioles are present throughout the cell (asterisk in Figure 4B).
evidence: This is quantification of electron microscopy measurements shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Centrioles are present throughout the cell in talpid3 choroid plexus.
source: In contrast, the mitochondria in talpid3 choroid plexus are found in the most apical zone, an average of 3 µm from the apical surface (m, Figure 4B), and centrioles are present throughout the cell (asterisk in Figure 4B).
evidence: This is an observation from electron microscopy shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The neuroepithelium of talpid3 choroid plexus has an abnormal intracellular organization of centrosomes and mitochondria and is not correctly polarized.
source: We conclude that the neuroepithelium has an abnormal intracellular organization of centrosomes and mitochondria and therefore, like the HCs and migratory fibroblasts, is not correctly polarized.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the electron microscopy data.

claim: Subdistal appendages were identified in approximately 40% of wildtype and talpid3 centrioles (wt n = 35, talpid3 n = 48).
source: Subdistal appendages were identified in approximately 40% of wildtype and talpid3 centrioles (wt n = 35, talpid3 n = 48, Figure 4D,E,G), whereas distal appendages were noted in 28% of wildtype centrioles and only 6% of talpid3 centrioles (Figure 4D–G).
evidence: This is quantification of electron microscopy observations.

claim: Distal appendages were noted in 28% of wildtype centrioles and only 6% of talpid3 centrioles.
source: Subdistal appendages were identified in approximately 40% of wildtype and talpid3 centrioles (wt n = 35, talpid3 n = 48, Figure 4D,E,G), whereas distal appendages were noted in 28% of wildtype centrioles and only 6% of talpid3 centrioles (Figure 4D–G).
evidence: This is quantification of electron microscopy observations.

claim: CEP164 localized correctly at the mother centriole and not at the sister centriole, in both wildtype and talpid3 cells of the neuroepithelium and fibroblasts.
source: CEP164 localized correctly at the mother centriole and not at the sister centriole, in both wildtype and talpid3 cells of the neuroepithelium and fibroblasts (Figure 4H–M).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence shown in Figure 4H–M.

claim: CEP164 puncta were smaller, disorganized and frequently orientated away from the apical cell surface in talpid3 cells.
source: However, CEP164 puncta were smaller, disorganized and frequently orientated away from the apical cell surface in talpid3 cells (Figure 4K,L).
evidence: This is an observation from immunofluorescence shown in Figure 4K,L.

claim: Smaller sized CEP164 puncta suggested that distal appendages were not formed normally in talpid3 cells.
source: Smaller sized CEP164 puncta also suggested that distal appendages were not formed normally in talpid3 cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the CEP164 immunofluorescence data.

claim: Centrioles in wildtype choroid plexus tissue were on average 0.7 µm in length compared to 0.9 µm in the talpid3 chicken.
source: Centrioles in wildtype tissue were on average 0.7 µm in length compared to 0.9 µm in the talpid3 chicken, suggesting that talpid3 centrioles may indeed fail to undergo complete maturation and are subsequently elongated (Figure 4R).
evidence: This is quantification of centriole length measurements shown in Figure 4R.

claim: Talpid3 centrioles may fail to undergo complete maturation and are subsequently elongated.
source: Centrioles in wildtype tissue were on average 0.7 µm in length compared to 0.9 µm in the talpid3 chicken, suggesting that talpid3 centrioles may indeed fail to undergo complete maturation and are subsequently elongated (Figure 4R).
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the centriole length data.

claim: In human cells, KIAA0586 is required for centriolar satellite dispersal.
source: In human cells, KIAA0586 is also required for centriolar satellite dispersal (Kobayashi et al., 2014a).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Electron-dense condensations were observed around the centrioles in the neuroepithelium of talpid3 chicken, which were absent from wildtype centrioles.
source: Compatible with this, we observed electron-dense condensations around the centrioles in the neuroepithelium of talpid3 chicken, which were absent from wildtype centrioles (basal body; 80% of wildtype cell exhibited electron-dense clear area around the centriole, whereas only 21% of talpid3 cells did; wt n = 35, talpid3 n = 48; Figure 5A,D,G).
evidence: This is an observation from electron microscopy shown in Figure 5A,D,G.

claim: 80% of wildtype choroid plexus cells exhibited electron-dense clear area around the centriole, whereas only 21% of talpid3 cells did (wt n = 35, talpid3 n = 48).
source: Compatible with this, we observed electron-dense condensations around the centrioles in the neuroepithelium of talpid3 chicken, which were absent from wildtype centrioles (basal body; 80% of wildtype cell exhibited electron-dense clear area around the centriole, whereas only 21% of talpid3 cells did; wt n = 35, talpid3 n = 48; Figure 5A,D,G).
evidence: This is quantification of electron microscopy observations.

claim: PCM1 puncta were larger around talpid3 centrioles compared to wildtype centrioles.
source: To determine if these were centriolar satellites, we examined the localization of PCM1, a marker for centriolar satellites. Compared to wildtype centrioles (Figure 5B,C), PCM1 puncta were larger around talpid3 centrioles (Figure 5E,F), possibly reflecting an increase in centriolar satellites.
evidence: This is an observation from immunofluorescence shown in Figure 5E,F.

claim: Larger PCM1 puncta around talpid3 centrioles possibly reflect an increase in centriolar satellites.
source: Compared to wildtype centrioles (Figure 5B,C), PCM1 puncta were larger around talpid3 centrioles (Figure 5E,F), possibly reflecting an increase in centriolar satellites.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the PCM1 immunofluorescence data.

claim: KIAA0586 and AZI1 did not colocalize in human RPE1 cells.
source: Because we observed KIAA0586 immunostaining around the pericentriolar region (Figure 2G,H), we used the centriolar satellite marker AZI1 in human RPE1 cells to determine if KIAA0586 localized to centriolar satellites (Figure 5H–J) but found that KIAA0586 and AZI1 did not colocalize.
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence shown in Figure 5H–J.

claim: TALPID3 is essential for centriolar satellite dispersal, and this is an indirect consequence of TALPID3 deficiency because TALPID3 protein does not localize to the centriolar satellites.
source: Thus, as observed in human cell lines, TALPID3 is essential for centriolar satellite dispersal. As TALPID3 protein does not localize to the centriolar satellites, we assume that this is an indirect consequence of TALPID3 deficiency.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the localization and satellite dispersal data.

claim: KIAA0586 (TALPID3) is essential for centriole migration and orientation which can subsequently affect cell and tissue polarity and ciliogenesis.

claim: KIAA0586 (TALPID3) is essential for centriole maturation which affects docking of the basal body and ciliogenesis.
source: We conclude that KIAA0586 (TALPID3) is essential for several distinct roles in centriole function, including centriole migration and orientation which can subsequently affect cell and tissue polarity and ciliogenesis, centriole maturation which affects docking of the basal body and ciliogenesis and through an indirect mechanism, centriolar satellite dispersal, which may also affect ciliogenesis.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on all the experimental data.

claim: JBTS is a genetically heterogeneous condition, caused by mutations in several genes related to the structure and function of cilia.

claim: A novel disease locus (JBTS23) was identified, defined by mutations in the KIAA0586 gene, encoding a centrosomal protein.
source: Through homozygosity mapping and WES, we identified a novel disease locus (JBTS23), defined by mutations in the KIAA0586 gene, encoding a centrosomal protein (Andersen et al., 2003) (Figure 1), which is supported by simultaneous concurrent studies (Bachmann-Gagescu et al., 2015; Roosing et al., 2015).

claim: The identification of JBTS23 is supported by simultaneous concurrent studies.

claim: Loss of KIAA0586 (TALPID3) function in animal models causes abnormal tissue polarity, centrosome length and orientation, and centriolar satellites.

claim: KIAA0586 has previously been associated with recessive ciliopathy phenotypes in mouse, chicken and zebrafish.
source: KIAA0586 has previously been associated with recessive ciliopathy phenotypes in mouse (Bangs et al., 2011; Davey et al., 2014), chicken (Davey et al., 2006; Davey et al., 2007) and zebrafish (Ben et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Animal models with naturally occurring or induced 5′ mutations in KIAA0586 that disrupt an essential coiled-coil domain result in loss of protein function, consecutive loss of Hh signaling and early embryonic lethality.

evidence: This is based on previous studies of animal models.

claim: The talpid3 chicken has polydactyly, holoprosencephaly, abnormal neural tube patterning, polycystic kidneys, liver fibrosis, short ribs, and endochondral bones with defective ossification.
source: The talpid3 chicken is a thoroughly examined animal model with polydactyly, holoprosencephaly, abnormal neural tube patterning, polycystic kidneys, liver fibrosis, short ribs, and endochondral bones with defective ossification (Lewis et al., 1999; Buxton et al., 2004; Davey et al., 2006; Davey et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The c.428delG (p.Arg143Lysfs*4) mutation was identified in heterozygous state in patient MD1, in trans to a nonsense mutation.

claim: The c.428delG mutation results in a premature termination codon in five human KIAA0586 isoforms, causing either a major protein truncation 5′ to the essential coiled-coil domain or NMD.
source: The c.428delG mutation results in a premature termination codon in five human KIAA0586 isoforms, causing either a major protein truncation 5′ to the essential coiled-coil domain or NMD.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and prediction of protein consequences.

claim: The c.428delG mutation is comparable to the talpid3 chicken loss-of-function mutation which introduces a frameshift in the orthologous region.
source: It is comparable to the talpid3 chicken loss-of-function mutation which introduces a frameshift in the orthologous region (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is based on sequence comparison between human and chicken orthologs.

claim: The c.428delG mutation is annotated in dbSNP (rs534542684), and its MAF in the general population is surprisingly high (0.39%, 378 out of 96,534 alleles in the ExAC db).
source: The c.428delG mutation is annotated in dbSNP (rs534542684), and its MAF in the general population is surprisingly high (0.39%, 378 out of 96,534 alleles in the ExAC db), reminiscent of the most common deafness (c.35delG in GJB2; 0.60% in the ExAC database) or cystic fibrosis (p.Phe508del in CFTR; 0.67% in the ExAC database) mutation.
evidence: This is based on database searches and comparison to other common disease mutations.

claim: In two concurrent studies reporting KIAA0586 mutations in patients with JBTS, c.428delG represented the most prevalent mutation.
source: In two concurrent studies reporting KIAA0586 mutations in patients with JBTS, c.428delG represented the most prevalent mutation (Bachmann-Gagescu et al., 2015; Roosing et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to concurrent studies.

claim: c.428delG was clearly enriched in patients with biallelic KIAA0586 mutations (present in 20 of 24 such patients), but only two were homozygous.
source: While c.428delG was clearly enriched in patients with biallelic KIAA0586 mutations in both studies (present in 20 of 24 such patients), only two were homozygous.
evidence: This is based on data from concurrent studies.

claim: Despite its commonness, c.428delG was not observed in homozygous state in healthy individuals in the TGP, ESP, or ExAC databases.
source: Despite its commonness, c.428delG was neither observed in homozygous state in healthy individuals in the TGP, ESP, or ExAC databases.
evidence: This is based on database searches.

claim: Rarity of homozygosity for c.428delG could indicate that it causes embryonic lethality, early death or severe illness leading to underrepresentation of the respective samples.
source: Such rarity of homozygosity could indicate that it causes embryonic lethality, early death or severe illness leading to underrepresentation of the respective samples.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the database data.

claim: Embryonic lethality in talpid3 chicken and Talpid3−/− knockout mice would support the interpretation that c.428delG causes embryonic lethality or early death.
source: Embryonic lethality in talpid3 chicken and Talpid3−/− knockout mice would support such an interpretation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the animal model phenotypes.

claim: c.428delG was not found in a simultaneous study that reports biallelic KIAA0586 mutations in early lethal ciliopathies.
source: On the other hand, c.428delG was not found in a simultaneous study that reports biallelic KIAA0586 mutations in early lethal ciliopathies (Alby et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a concurrent study.

claim: A very recent study on rare human knockouts identified one individual of 57 years with homozygosity for c.428delG.
source: Of note, a very recent study on rare human knockouts identified in the genomes of 2636 healthy Icelanders lists one individual of 57 years with homozygosity for c.428delG (Sulem et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a recent study.

claim: Homozygosity for c.428delG in a healthy individual could be due to protective modifiers or a low mutational load in the ciliome.
source: This could either be due to protective modifiers or a low mutational load in the ciliome of the respective person.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the finding of a healthy homozygous individual.

claim: c.428delGKIAA0586 could represent a hypomorphic allele that increases susceptibility to develop JBTS, with more severe mutations required either in trans or in other genes for disease manifestation.

(2015); Roosing et al. (2015)), or in other genes (in homozygous carriers) for disease manifestation.
evidence: This is a hypothesis to explain the genetic findings and the presence of a healthy homozygous individual.

source: The presence of a heterozygous potentially deleterious C5orf42 (JBTS17) variant in the only c.428delGKIAA0586-homozygous patient reported by Bachmann-Gagescu et al. evidence: This is an inference based on the genetic findings in patients.

claim: No secondary KIAA0586 mutation was identified in c.428delG-heterozygous JBTS patients in two other studies, which could be due to the contribution of other genes.
source: Of note, no secondary KIAA0586 mutation was identified in c.428delG-heterozygous JBTS patients in the two other studies (Bachmann-Gagescu et al., 2015; Roosing et al., 2015), which could be due to the contribution of other genes.
evidence: This is based on data from concurrent studies and is a speculative interpretation.

claim: The homozygous mutations c.2414-1G>C (Family 1) and c.2512C>T (p.Arg838*, Family 2) would not disrupt the 5′ functionally essential coiled-coil domain in the consecutive KIAA0586 protein, and partial function may be maintained.

claim: KIAA0586 has several functions in the centriole, and this may be mediated by different protein residues.
source: We have shown that KIAA0586 has several functions in the centriole, and this may be mediated by different protein residues.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the functional data from the study.

claim: The occurrence of retinal degeneration in JBTS depends on the genetic subtype, but is variable even within a family.
source: The occurrence of retinal degeneration in JBTS depends on the genetic subtype, but is variable even within a family.
evidence: This is based on established clinical knowledge about JBTS.

claim: The localization of KIAA0586 at the ciliary base of retinal photoreceptor cells corresponds to other JBTS proteins.
source: The localization of KIAA0586 at the ciliary base of retinal photoreceptor cells corresponds to other JBTS proteins.
evidence: This is based on comparison to known localization of other JBTS proteins.

source: Proteins of the periciliary compartment at the base of the photoreceptor cilium are thought to be critical for the handover of cargo from the dynein-mediated transport through the inner segment to the kinesin-powered anterograde intraflagellar transport in the ciliary compartment (Roepman and Wolfrum, 2007; Sedmak and Wolfrum, 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: KIAA0586 may be part of the protein networks implicated in cargo handover at the photoreceptor ciliary base.
source: KIAA0586 may be part of the protein networks implicated in these processes.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the localization of KIAA0586.

claim: The lack of retinal disease in the patients described may be due to the less strongly developed structure of the distal appendages and/or the possible functional redundancy in the cilia of retinal photoreceptor cells.
source: The lack of retinal disease in the patients described herein may be due to the less strongly developed structure of the distal appendages and/or the possible functional redundancy in the cilia of retinal photoreceptor cells.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the lack of retinal disease in the patients.

claim: Patients with KIAA0586-related JBTS should be investigated for signs of retinal degeneration.
source: Nevertheless, patients with KIAA0586-related JBTS should be investigated for signs of retinal degeneration, and given that mutations in the JBTS gene CEP290 may cause non-syndromic Leber congenital amaurosis (den Hollander et al., 2006), KIAA0586 represents a candidate gene for isolated retinopathies.
evidence: This is a clinical recommendation based on the findings and comparison to other JBTS genes.

claim: KIAA0586 represents a candidate gene for isolated retinopathies.
source: Nevertheless, patients with KIAA0586-related JBTS should be investigated for signs of retinal degeneration, and given that mutations in the JBTS gene CEP290 may cause non-syndromic Leber congenital amaurosis (den Hollander et al., 2006), KIAA0586 represents a candidate gene for isolated retinopathies.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on comparison to CEP290.

claim: Most patients with KIAA0586-related JBTS exhibit few classical Hh phenotypes such as polydactyly.
source: Most patients with KIAA0586-related JBTS exhibit few classical Hh phenotypes such as polydactyly (this study, Bachmann-Gagescu et al., 2015; Roosing et al., 2015), unlike the corresponding mouse, chicken, and zebrafish models (Davey et al., 2006; Bangs et al., 2011; Ben et al., 2011).
evidence: This is based on clinical observations from this study and concurrent studies.

claim: Cell and tissue polarity are disrupted upon loss of TALPID3, independent of Hh signaling.
source: We show that, independent of Hh signaling, cell and tissue polarity are disrupted upon loss of TALPID3.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on experiments in animal models.

source: JBTS is characterized by cerebellar hypoplasia and loss of decussation of neuronal projections from the cerebellum (Romani et al., 2013).

claim: Hh signaling is required for controlling the growth of the embryonic cerebellar primordia.

evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The failure of decussation in JBTS has been proposed to result from defective axonal guidance, a process depending on centrosome-guided cell polarity.
source: While Hh signaling is required for controlling the growth of the embryonic cerebellar primordia (Lewis et al., 2004), the failure of decussation has been proposed to result from defective axonal guidance (Romani et al., 2013), a process depending on centrosome-guided cell polarity (Solecki et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In inner ear hair cells, cell polarity and ciliogenesis, albeit closely linked, are differentially affected in talpid3 cells.
source: Furthermore, we have shown that in inner ear HCs, cell polarity and ciliogenesis, albeit closely linked, are differentially affected in talpid3 cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the hair cell data.
